title: Trunking and 802.1Q: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Two switches. Ten different floors. Just one cable between them. So how does the mail avoid getting mixed up?

scenes.heading: The colour-coded mailroom
scenes.narration: Picture a mail carrier delivering letters for every floor of a building. Each letter gets a coloured sticker saying which floor it belongs to. That sticker is a small tag defined by the standard called eight oh two dot one Q. The cable between the two mailrooms is the trunk. Letters for the default floor travel with no sticker at all. That default floor is the native V L A N.

scenes.heading: Trunk commands
scenes.narration: The commands are short. Force the port to be a trunk. Limit which floors are allowed through. And check the result with show interfaces trunk.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Watch for three slip-ups. Frames on the native V L A N travel untagged. Both ends must agree on the native V L A N, or traffic leaks. And two ports set to dynamic auto will never form a trunk.

items.wrong: Every frame on a trunk is tagged
Native VLAN can differ per side
items.right: Both ends must match or traffic leaks

items.wrong: Two dynamic auto ports make a trunk
items.right: One side must be trunk or desirable

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A trunk carries many V L A N over one cable, using little tags. The native V L A N goes untagged, and both ends must match. And never rely on dynamic auto at both ends. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva trunking lab.

points.t: A trunk carries many VLANs using 802.1Q tags
Never dynamic auto on both ends
